questions.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes is prescribed regular insulin 6 units and NPH insulin 14 units subcutaneously before breakfast, given in one syringe. Place the steps for preparing the injection in order, from first to last.

items.text: Inject 14 units of air into the NPH vial without withdrawing insulin
Withdraw 14 units of NPH insulin into the same syringe, for a total of 20 units
Inject 6 units of air into the regular insulin vial

rationale.correct: Air into cloudy, air into clear, draw clear, then draw cloudy. This keeps intermediate-acting insulin out of the regular insulin vial.

perOption.a: Air goes into the cloudy (NPH) vial first, so the needle never touches NPH before drawing regular insulin.
perOption.b: Adding air to the regular vial makes withdrawal easier.
perOption.c: Clear (regular) insulin is drawn up first so it isn't contaminated with NPH.
perOption.d: Cloudy insulin is drawn last.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Mix regular and NPH insulin in one syringe correctly.

questions.stem: A client newly started on NPH insulin 24 units subcutaneously at 0700 eats breakfast at 0800, lunch at 1230 and dinner at 1800. During which period is the client at greatest risk for hypoglycemia from this dose?

rationale.correct: Hypoglycemia is most likely during an insulin's peak. NPH peaks 4 to 12 hours after injection, so a morning dose peaks from late morning to early evening.

perOption.a: NPH starts working 1 to 2 hours after injection and is not near its peak yet.
perOption.b: NPH peaks about 4 to 12 hours after injection, so a missed or late lunch or afternoon activity is risky.
perOption.c: By late evening the peak of a morning dose is wearing off.
perOption.d: Overnight lows are a risk with an evening NPH dose, not a morning one.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Link insulin peak times to hypoglycemia risk.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client with type 1 diabetes who has started insulin glargine at bedtime and insulin lispro with meals. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll take the glargine at about the same time every night."
"I'll draw the lispro into the glargine syringe to save a shot."
"The glargine works all day and doesn't have a strong peak."
"I'll take the lispro when my meal is in front of me."

rationale.correct: Long-acting insulin analogs such as glargine and detemir are never mixed with other insulins.

perOption.a: Consistent timing keeps basal insulin levels steady.
perOption.b: Glargine must never be mixed with another insulin; mixing changes its absorption.
perOption.c: Glargine is a basal insulin with no pronounced peak.
perOption.d: Lispro acts within about 15 minutes, so it is given with the meal.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach safe use of long-acting insulin.

questions.stem: A client with diabetic ketoacidosis has been on an IV regular insulin infusion and 0.9% sodium chloride for 6 hours. The glucose is now 238 mg/dL, potassium 3.9 mEq/L, bicarbonate 13 mEq/L and anion gap 19. Which prescription should the nurse anticipate next?

options.text: Stop the insulin infusion and start correction-scale subcutaneous insulin
Change the IV fluid to one with dextrose and continue the insulin infusion
Give IV sodium bicarbonate to correct the bicarbonate of 13 mEq/L
Stop the potassium in the IV fluid now that the level is normal

rationale.correct: In DKA, the insulin infusion treats the ketoacidosis, not just the glucose. Add dextrose when glucose nears 200 to 250 mg/dL and continue insulin until the anion gap closes.

perOption.a: The acidosis has not resolved (gap still high), so the infusion must continue; stopping it would let ketones build up again.
perOption.b: When glucose falls to about 200 to 250 mg/dL, dextrose is added so insulin can continue until the anion gap closes.
perOption.c: Bicarbonate is reserved for very severe acidosis (pH below about 6.9).
perOption.d: Insulin keeps driving potassium into cells; replacement continues to keep it between 4 and 5 mEq/L.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
American Diabetes Association Standards of Care
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Anticipate fluid and insulin changes during DKA treatment.

questions.stem: A client with diabetic ketoacidosis who weighs 70 kg is prescribed a regular insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hr. The pharmacy sends a bag containing 100 units of regular insulin in 100 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride. At what rate should the nurse set the infusion pump?

rationale.correct: Dose: 0.1 units/kg/hr × 70 kg = 7 units/hr. Concentration: 100 units ÷ 100 mL = 1 unit/mL. Rate: 7 units/hr ÷ 1 unit/mL = 7 mL/hr.
references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Calculate a weight-based insulin infusion rate.

questions.stem: A client with type 1 diabetes is due for prescribed insulin lispro 6 units with lunch. The lunch tray has arrived. The client's fingerstick glucose is 52 mg/dL, and the client is alert, sweaty and able to swallow. Complete the sentence.

content.template: The nurse should {{b1}} the scheduled lispro and first {{b2}}.

options.text: hold
give
halve
give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate and recheck the glucose in 15 minutes
give 1 mg of glucagon IM
give the lunch tray, because the meal contains carbohydrate

rationale.correct: Treat hypoglycemia before giving rapid-acting insulin, and contact the provider about adjusting the dose.

perOption.b1:a: Giving rapid-acting insulin with a glucose of 52 mg/dL would deepen the hypoglycemia.
perOption.b1:b: Lispro lowers glucose within 15 minutes and would make the hypoglycemia worse.
perOption.b1:c: Any rapid-acting insulin now worsens the low; the glucose is treated first.
perOption.b2:a: The 15-15 rule treats hypoglycemia in an alert client who can swallow.
perOption.b2:b: Glucagon is for clients who cannot swallow safely.
perOption.b2:c: A mixed meal with fat and protein raises glucose too slowly to treat a low.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
American Diabetes Association Standards of Care
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to hypoglycemia before giving mealtime insulin.

questions.stem: A client using a morphine PCA pump after a hip replacement is hard to rouse, responds only to a firm shoulder shake, and has a respiratory rate of 7/min and an SpO2 of 86% on room air. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Apply oxygen at 2 L/min by nasal cannula and reassess in 15 minutes
Stop the PCA, keep stimulating the client and prepare naloxone
Halve the PCA demand dose and lengthen the lockout interval
Review the PCA history to see how many doses the client used

rationale.correct: Sedation comes before respiratory depression. Stop the opioid, stimulate the client, support breathing and give naloxone per protocol.

perOption.a: Oxygen helps the saturation but does nothing for the opioid that is suppressing the drive to breathe.
perOption.b: Stopping the opioid, rousing the client and reversing with naloxone treats opioid-induced respiratory depression.
perOption.c: Any further opioid could deepen the respiratory depression.
perOption.d: The history matters later; the client needs treatment now.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to opioid-induced respiratory depression.

questions.stem: The nurse gave naloxone 0.4 mg IV to a client with respiratory depression after IV morphine. Five minutes later the client is awake, reports pain of 6 out of 10 and has a respiratory rate of 14/min. What is the main reason the nurse must keep monitoring breathing closely for the next few hours?

options.text: Naloxone can trigger pain and withdrawal, which raise heart rate and blood pressure
Naloxone wears off in 30 to 90 minutes, before the morphine, so sedation can return
Naloxone often causes delayed pulmonary edema in clients who have had surgery
Naloxone slows the liver's breakdown of morphine, which raises its level later

rationale.correct: Because naloxone acts for a shorter time than many opioids, watch for re-sedation and respiratory depression and be ready to repeat the dose.

perOption.a: Withdrawal and pain can happen and are watched for, but they are not the main danger to breathing.
perOption.b: Naloxone's short half-life means respiratory depression can recur, so repeat doses may be needed.
perOption.c: Pulmonary edema after naloxone is rare.
perOption.d: Naloxone blocks opioid receptors; it does not change how morphine is metabolized.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Monitor for recurrent sedation after naloxone.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old client who lives with two teenagers is going home after spinal surgery with oxycodone extended-release twice a day and immediate-release oxycodone for breakthrough pain. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Take a stool softener and laxative as prescribed and drink plenty of fluids
Avoid alcohol, sleep aids and other sedating medications
Keep the tablets in a locked place that the teenagers cannot reach
Crush the extended-release tablet if it is too large to swallow
Take an extra extended-release tablet if the pain is not relieved
Stop the laxative once the first bowel movement happens at home

rationale.correct: Opioid teaching covers ongoing constipation prevention, avoiding other depressants, secure storage and never altering or adding long-acting doses.

perOption.a: Opioids slow the bowel, and constipation does not improve with time.
perOption.b: Combining depressants raises the risk of respiratory depression.
perOption.c: Secure storage prevents misuse by others in the home.
perOption.d: Crushing releases the whole dose at once and can be fatal.
perOption.e: Extra long-acting doses cause overdose; the client uses the breakthrough dose or calls the provider.
perOption.f: Constipation continues while opioids are taken, so the bowel regimen continues too.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with chronic cancer pain has been prescribed a transdermal fentanyl patch every 72 hours. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll take off the old patch before I put on a new one."
"I'll put a heating pad on my back when the pain flares."
"I'll fold the used patch sticky sides together and flush it."
"I'll put each new patch on a different area of clean skin."

rationale.correct: Heat from heating pads, hot tubs, saunas or fever speeds up fentanyl absorption and can cause dangerous toxicity.

perOption.a: Removing the old patch prevents a double dose.
perOption.b: Heat increases fentanyl absorption and can cause overdose.
perOption.c: Folding and disposing of the patch as instructed prevents accidental exposure.
perOption.d: Rotating sites prevents skin irritation.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach safe use of transdermal fentanyl.

questions.stem: A client with vomiting has a potassium level of 3.1 mEq/L, and the provider prescribes potassium chloride 10 mEq in 100 mL over 1 hour through a peripheral IV. Which finding should cause the nurse to hold the infusion and contact the provider?

options.text: Urine output of 90 mL over the last 6 hours
Flattened T waves and U waves on the cardiac monitor
A 20-gauge forearm IV with a brisk blood return
A serum magnesium level of 1.9 mg/dL

rationale.correct: Before IV potassium, confirm the kidneys can excrete it: urine output of at least 30 mL/hr. Never give potassium IV push, and always dilute it and use a pump.

perOption.a: Output of about 15 mL/hr suggests poor kidney function, and potassium given without adequate output can cause dangerous hyperkalemia.
perOption.b: These ECG changes are expected with hypokalemia and are a reason to replace potassium.
perOption.c: A patent peripheral IV is acceptable for this dilute concentration given slowly.
perOption.d: This magnesium level is normal; low magnesium would make potassium harder to correct.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Assess kidney function before giving IV potassium.

questions.stem: The nurse observes a nursing student giving enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously from a prefilled syringe to a client after knee surgery. Which action by the student requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: Chooses a site on the abdomen at least 5 cm (2 inches) from the navel
Leaves the air bubble in the prefilled syringe before injecting
Pulls back on the plunger to check for blood before injecting
Holds the skin fold until the injection is complete

rationale.correct: For enoxaparin: do not expel the air bubble, do not aspirate, inject into a pinched fold on the abdomen, and do not rub the site.

perOption.a: This is the correct site for enoxaparin.
perOption.b: The bubble is left in so the full dose is given.
perOption.c: Aspirating with anticoagulants damages tissue and causes bruising; it is not done.
perOption.d: Keeping the skin fold pinched throughout is correct technique.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Give low-molecular-weight heparin correctly.

questions.stem: The rapid response nurse is preparing for possible drug toxicity in five clients. For each drug, select the antidote or reversal agent the nurse should expect to give.

options.text: Idarucizumab
Vitamin K
Protamine sulfate
Andexanet alfa
Protamine sulfate
Vitamin K
Idarucizumab
Flumazenil
Digoxin immune fab
Atropine
Glucagon
Naloxone
Calcium gluconate
Sodium bicarbonate
Protamine sulfate
Flumazenil
Naloxone
Flumazenil
Calcium gluconate
Glucagon

rationale.correct: Know the common antidotes: idarucizumab (dabigatran), andexanet (factor Xa inhibitors), protamine (heparin), vitamin K (warfarin), digoxin immune fab (digoxin), calcium gluconate (magnesium), flumazenil (benzodiazepines), naloxone (opioids).

perOption.b1:a: Idarucizumab binds dabigatran and reverses it.
perOption.b1:d: Andexanet reverses factor Xa inhibitors such as apixaban.
perOption.b2:a: Protamine binds heparin and neutralizes it.
perOption.b3:b: Atropine treats symptomatic bradycardia but does not reverse digoxin.
perOption.b3:c: Glucagon is used for beta-blocker toxicity.
perOption.b4:b: Bicarbonate treats some acidosis and tricyclic toxicity.
perOption.b5:d: Glucagon treats hypoglycemia and beta-blocker toxicity.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Match drugs to their antidotes.

questions.stem: A client taking warfarin 5 mg daily for atrial fibrillation has an INR of 5.2 this morning. The client has no bleeding, bruising or dark stools. The evening warfarin dose is due. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the dose, because the client has no signs of bleeding
Hold the warfarin dose and notify the provider of the INR
Give protamine sulfate as the reversal agent for warfarin
Give half the dose tonight and recheck the INR tomorrow

rationale.correct: Hold warfarin for a supratherapeutic INR and notify the provider. The target INR for atrial fibrillation is 2 to 3.

perOption.a: More warfarin with an INR well above target raises the risk of bleeding.
perOption.b: The INR is above the 2 to 3 target; the dose is held and the provider decides on next steps, such as low-dose oral vitamin K.
perOption.c: Protamine reverses heparin, not warfarin.
perOption.d: The nurse cannot change the dose without a prescription.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a high INR in a client taking warfarin.

questions.stem: A client who took warfarin for years is switched to apixaban for atrial fibrillation. The client asks, "How often will I need my blood checked now?" What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "You'll have an INR check every week for the first month."
"You won't need regular INR checks with this medicine."
"You'll need a monthly anti-Xa level to adjust your dose."
"Only if you change how many leafy green vegetables you eat."

rationale.correct: DOACs such as apixaban, rivaroxaban and dabigatran do not need routine INR monitoring. Clients still need bleeding precautions and periodic kidney function tests.

perOption.a: INR does not measure the effect of apixaban.
perOption.b: Direct oral anticoagulants have predictable effects and do not need routine INR checks; kidney function is still checked periodically.
perOption.c: Routine drug-level monitoring is not needed for apixaban.
perOption.d: Vitamin K intake affects warfarin, not apixaban.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach a client about monitoring direct oral anticoagulants.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old client arrives with right-sided weakness and aphasia that began 2 hours ago. A CT scan shows no bleeding, and the team is considering IV alteplase. Which finding makes alteplase contraindicated?

options.text: Blood pressure of 178/100 mm Hg
Platelet count of 80,000/mm3
INR of 1.4 in a client who takes no anticoagulant
Glucose of 62 mg/dL that was treated, now 110 mg/dL

rationale.correct: Before a thrombolytic, check for bleeding risks: platelets under 100,000/mm3, INR over 1.7, pressure above 185/110 mm Hg, recent surgery, bleeding or intracranial hemorrhage.

perOption.a: Alteplase can be given if the pressure is below 185/110 mm Hg.
perOption.b: A platelet count below 100,000/mm3 makes bleeding too likely, so alteplase is contraindicated.
perOption.c: An INR up to 1.7 is acceptable for alteplase.
perOption.d: Glucose is checked because hypoglycemia can mimic a stroke; once corrected it is not a contraindication.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify contraindications to thrombolytic therapy.

questions.stem: A client receiving IV gentamicin for 5 days reports ringing in both ears and feeling unsteady when walking. The next dose is due in 1 hour. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Draw the trough level before the dose and give it if the level is in range
Hold the next dose and notify the provider of the new symptoms
Explain that ringing in the ears is common and goes away after treatment
Give the next dose over a longer time to lower the peak level

rationale.correct: Aminoglycosides can cause ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity. Monitor hearing, balance, creatinine and drug levels, and report symptoms before the next dose.

perOption.a: The level matters, but new symptoms of toxicity need the provider's review before another dose.
perOption.b: Tinnitus and unsteadiness suggest ototoxicity, which can become permanent; the provider may change the drug or dose.
perOption.c: Aminoglycoside ototoxicity is often permanent and is not expected.
perOption.d: The nurse cannot change the administration without a prescription, and the symptoms need review first.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize aminoglycoside ototoxicity.

questions.stem: Ten minutes after a unit of packed red blood cells is started, a client reports chills and low back pain. The temperature has risen from 37.0 °C to 38.5 °C (98.6 °F to 101.3 °F), and the heart rate is 118/min. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Slow the transfusion to the lowest rate and recheck vital signs in 15 minutes
Stop the blood and run 0.9% sodium chloride through new tubing
Give the PRN diphenhydramine and acetaminophen, then continue the unit
Call the blood bank and send the bag and tubing back for testing

rationale.correct: For any suspected transfusion reaction: stop the transfusion, keep the vein open with saline through new tubing, notify the provider and the blood bank, and monitor the client.

perOption.a: Slowing a possible hemolytic reaction still lets incompatible blood in.
perOption.b: Stopping the blood limits the reaction, and new tubing avoids giving the blood left in the line.
perOption.c: Premedication is for mild allergic or febrile reactions; back pain with fever suggests hemolysis.
perOption.d: The bag and tubing are returned, but only after the client is safe.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a suspected transfusion reaction.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old client with heart failure and a hemoglobin of 6.9 g/dL is to receive a unit of packed red blood cells. Which actions by the nurse are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Check the client and unit identification with another licensed nurse at the bedside
Prime the blood tubing with 0.9% sodium chloride
Use blood tubing with an in-line filter
Stay with the client for the first 15 minutes of the transfusion
Infuse the unit over 6 hours to prevent fluid overload
Prime the tubing with D5W to keep the vein open
Run the blood through the line used for the client's antibiotics

rationale.correct: Safe transfusion: verified identity, normal saline only, filtered tubing, close early monitoring and completion within 4 hours.

perOption.a: A two-person bedside check prevents ABO-incompatible transfusions.
perOption.b: Only normal saline is compatible with blood.
perOption.c: A filter removes clots and debris.
perOption.d: Most severe reactions happen early.
perOption.e: A unit must be finished within 4 hours to limit bacterial growth; the bank can split it if needed.
perOption.f: Dextrose solutions cause red blood cells to clump and hemolyze.
perOption.g: Blood is not given with other drugs in the same line.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prepare to give a blood transfusion safely.

questions.stem: A client receiving total parenteral nutrition (TPN) at 85 mL/hr through a central line has an empty bag. The pharmacy says the next bag will be 2 hours late. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Flush the line and keep it capped until the new bag arrives
Hang 10% dextrose in water at the same rate as the TPN
Hang 0.9% sodium chloride at the same rate as the TPN
Run the next bag faster when it arrives to make up the volume

rationale.correct: Hang D10W if TPN is interrupted, never speed up TPN to catch up, and check glucose closely.

perOption.a: Stopping TPN suddenly can cause rebound hypoglycemia.
perOption.b: D10W keeps glucose flowing and prevents rebound hypoglycemia.
perOption.c: Saline does not provide glucose.
perOption.d: Catching up can cause hyperglycemia and fluid overload.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prevent hypoglycemia when TPN is interrupted.

questions.stem: While a client is being repositioned, the tubing separates from the hub of the client's subclavian central venous catheter. The client suddenly becomes short of breath, anxious and reports chest pain. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Clamp the catheter close to the insertion site
Turn the client onto the left side with the head down
Apply oxygen by nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min
Call the rapid response team to the bedside

rationale.correct: For suspected air embolism: clamp the catheter, put the client on the left side with the head down if not contraindicated, give oxygen and get help.

perOption.a: Clamping stops more air from entering the circulation.
perOption.b: This position traps air in the right atrium, but it follows clamping the catheter.
perOption.c: Oxygen is needed, but stopping more air from entering comes first.
perOption.d: Help is called right after the immediate action.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a suspected air embolism from a central line.

questions.stem: A client's peripheral IV site is cool, pale and swollen, and the infusion of 0.9% sodium chloride has slowed. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Stop the infusion, remove the catheter and raise the arm
Flush the catheter firmly to clear a possible clot
Apply a warm compress and keep the infusion running
Raise the IV bag higher to improve the flow rate

rationale.correct: Infiltration is cool, pale and swollen; phlebitis is warm, red and tender along the vein.

perOption.a: These findings indicate infiltration; the IV is stopped and removed and the arm raised.
perOption.b: Forceful flushing pushes more fluid into the tissue.
perOption.c: The infusion must be stopped first.
perOption.d: This forces more fluid into the tissue.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize and manage IV infiltration.

questions.stem: A client in septic shock is receiving norepinephrine through a peripheral IV in the forearm while a central line is being arranged. The nurse finds a cold, blanched area around the insertion site. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Stop the infusion at this site and get a prescription for local phentolamine
Apply ice to the site and continue the infusion while watching the area
Raise the infusion rate to keep the mean arterial pressure above 65 mm Hg
Massage the area gently to spread the drug and restore blood flow

rationale.correct: Vasopressor extravasation is treated by stopping the infusion at that site and giving phentolamine into the area; vasopressors are best given through a central line.

perOption.a: Norepinephrine leaking into tissue causes vasoconstriction and necrosis; phentolamine reverses the local vasoconstriction.
perOption.b: Ice worsens vasoconstriction, and the infusion must stop at that site.
perOption.c: This increases tissue damage at the site.
perOption.d: Massage spreads the drug and the damage.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Manage extravasation of a vasopressor.

questions.stem: The nurse is giving iron dextran by intramuscular injection to a client with iron-deficiency anemia who cannot take oral iron. Which technique should the nurse use?

options.text: The Z-track method into the ventrogluteal muscle
Massaging the site well after the injection
Injecting into the deltoid muscle of the arm
Using the needle that was used to draw up the drug

rationale.correct: Z-track injection keeps irritating or staining drugs from leaking into subcutaneous tissue.

perOption.a: The Z-track method seals the drug in the muscle, preventing leakage and skin staining.
perOption.b: Massage can push the drug into the subcutaneous tissue and stain the skin.
perOption.c: A large, deep muscle such as the ventrogluteal is preferred.
perOption.d: A new needle prevents tracking the irritating drug through the tissue.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Use the Z-track method for irritating IM medications.

questions.stem: The nurse is giving furosemide 80 mg by IV push to a client with acute heart failure and chronic kidney disease. Which action helps prevent ototoxicity?

options.text: Push the dose over at least 4 minutes, no faster than 20 mg/min
Push the dose over 30 seconds to get the quickest diuresis
Give the dose with a glass of milk to protect the stomach
Give half the dose IV and the other half intramuscularly

rationale.correct: Give IV furosemide slowly, no faster than about 20 mg/min; the risk of ototoxicity rises with fast or high doses and kidney disease.

perOption.a: Rapid IV push of high-dose furosemide raises the risk of ototoxicity, especially with kidney disease.
perOption.b: Rapid administration increases the risk of hearing damage.
perOption.c: Food does not affect IV furosemide.
perOption.d: Changing the route without a prescription is not appropriate.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.educationalObjective: Give IV push furosemide at a safe rate.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing 0900 medications for a client with heart failure and hypertension. Select the 3 assessments the nurse should check before giving these medications.

options.text: Blood pressure before giving lisinopril
Apical pulse for a full minute before giving digoxin
Potassium level before giving IV furosemide
Temperature before giving metoprolol
Blood glucose before giving amlodipine
Respiratory rate before giving atorvastatin

rationale.correct: Before giving cardiovascular drugs, check the vital sign or lab value the drug affects.

perOption.a: Lisinopril lowers blood pressure; hold it if the client is hypotensive.
perOption.b: Hold digoxin for a heart rate below 60/min, or per the prescriber's parameters.
perOption.c: Furosemide wastes potassium; hypokalemia must be corrected first.
perOption.d: Metoprolol needs a heart rate and blood pressure check.
perOption.e: Amlodipine needs a blood pressure check.
perOption.f: Statins need monitoring of liver function and muscle symptoms.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
